paragraphs: A change in camera position or a 3D scene can alter an image in structured ways that ordinary pixel noise does not capture. This paper introduces abstract rendering, which computes provable constraints covering every image produced within specified continuous variations of camera poses and scenes. The output represents a set of possible images.

The method carries camera uncertainty through the rendering pipeline using piecewise linear bounds. It introduces specialized treatments for matrix inversion, aggregation involving sorting, and cumulative product summation, operations that standard tools do not support. Those image constraints can then be propagated through a neural network to certify its behavior under the modeled 3D variations.

The implementation supports Gaussian Splats and neural radiance fields, including scenes with up to one million Gaussians. The authors report up to 3% over-approximation error relative to sampled results and demonstrate certification for classification, object detection, and pose estimation. The contribution connects uncertainty in a scene’s geometry and viewpoint to formal statements about downstream predictions.
neurips-2025-abstract-rendering-certifie.tldr: Abstract rendering bounds images under continuous 3D variations, enabling formal certification of downstream vision models.

paragraphs: Models that reconstruct 3D point clouds need a training loss that compares predicted points with target points. Common nearest-neighbor losses can assign many predictions to the same target, crowding dense areas while leaving sparse areas poorly covered. Exact one-to-one matching better captures structure, but Earth Mover Distance has cubic computational cost that limits its practical use.

Adaptive Probabilistic Matching Loss approximates one-to-one correspondence with soft assignment probabilities. It applies Sinkhorn iterations to a similarity matrix built from pairwise distances and scaled by a temperature. The temperature is calculated analytically to guarantee a minimum assignment probability, removing manual temperature tuning. The resulting loss is fully differentiable and has near-quadratic runtime.

The authors integrate the loss into several point-cloud architectures and a model that reconstructs human point clouds from WiFi measurements. Across these evaluations, they report faster convergence and better spatial distribution, particularly in low-density regions, with quantitative performance that improves or matches existing results. The approach makes more structured matching practical without additional hyperparameter search.
neurips-2025-apml-adaptive-probabilistic.tldr: APML uses differentiable probabilistic matching to improve point-cloud coverage while avoiding the cubic cost of exact matching.

paragraphs: Understanding how attention layers learn requires models that are mathematically manageable while retaining relevant architectural features. This paper introduces the attention-indexed model, a theoretical framework describing how token outputs arise from layered bilinear interactions among high-dimensional embeddings. It permits full-width key and query matrices, making its attention structure closer to practical transformers than earlier tractable models.

Using statistical mechanics and random matrix theory, the authors derive closed-form predictions for Bayes-optimal generalization error. These predictions describe the best performance under the framework’s Bayesian formulation. The analysis also identifies sharp changes in learning behavior as sample complexity, model width, and sequence length vary, connecting these quantities to transitions in achievable generalization.

The paper proposes an approximate message passing algorithm that matches the theoretical performance and shows that gradient descent can attain optimal performance. Together, these results provide both a performance characterization and algorithms capable of reaching it within the studied framework. AIM offers a solvable setting for investigating self-attention learning, with conclusions grounded in that theoretical model.
neurips-2025-bayes-optimal-learning-of-a.tldr: AIM provides a tractable attention model with explicit optimal-error predictions, learning phase transitions, and algorithms that can attain optimal performance.

paragraphs: An image prompt can leave many details unresolved, allowing multiple plausible outputs. Changing random seeds produces variation, but the differences can be difficult to interpret. Rewriting prompts offers more explicit control, yet limits diversity to distinctions that can be expressed in words. This paper instead represents uncertainty within the internal encoding of the condition.

The proposed framework inserts a latent graph, parameterized by Generative Flow Networks, into the computation of prompt representations. It samples multiple trajectories through that graph, with different trajectories capturing different aspects of the condition’s uncertainty. Each trajectory yields a distinct condition representation that can guide an image generator toward a corresponding plausible output.

The framework is described as applicable to any pretrained conditional generative model. Evaluations on natural and medical images report improvements in both diversity and fidelity across synthesis, generation, and counterfactual generation tasks. These findings suggest that explicitly organizing uncertainty in the conditioning representation can produce useful variation while preserving image quality, rather than relying solely on changes to random initialization.
neurips-2025-discovering-latent-graphs-w.tldr: A GFlowNet-based latent graph turns uncertain image conditions into varied representations, improving diversity and fidelity in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks require outputs to obey explicit rules, such as physical relationships or safety limits. A penalty for violating a rule does not itself ensure compliance. This paper develops a model-agnostic architecture for enforcing linear equality and inequality constraints whose requirements can depend on the input.

The architecture combines two subnetworks. A task network learns accurate predictions, while a safe network uses decision rules from stochastic and robust optimization to establish feasibility across the input space. The framework constructs the final output as a convex combination of their predictions, guaranteeing constraint satisfaction during training and inference. It does so without iterative correction or an optimization problem solved at prediction time.

The authors prove that the architecture can universally approximate constrained functions and derive computationally tractable versions using linear decision rules. On benchmark regression tasks, the method consistently meets its constraints while retaining competitive accuracy and low inference latency. The contribution therefore combines an architectural feasibility guarantee with evidence that enforcing the specified rules can remain computationally practical.
neurips-2025-enforcing-hard-linear-const.tldr: A task network and a decision-rule-based safe network jointly enforce input-dependent linear constraints without runtime optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies the quality of the final parameter setting produced by stochastic gradient descent. The setting is smooth convex optimization in the interpolation regime, where stochastic gradient noise at the optimum is zero or small. Understanding this final iterate matters for analyses of overparameterized learning, continual-learning forgetting, and randomized methods for solving linear systems.

The authors establish a population excess-risk bound for constant step sizes between zero and twice the reciprocal of the loss smoothness. The bound explicitly connects the step size, the number of updates, and gradient variance at the optimum. With a suitably tuned step size, they obtain a near-optimal rate consisting of a 1/T term and a noise-dependent term proportional to 1/√T, up to logarithmic factors.

When the noise at the optimum is exactly zero, choosing the reciprocal smoothness as the step size yields an O(1/√T) rate. This improves the cited O(T^−1/4) result for realizable linear regression. The analysis also extends previous tuned-step-size guarantees beyond least squares to smooth convex losses.
neurips-2025-fast-last-iterate-convergen.tldr: The paper strengthens final-iterate SGD guarantees for smooth convex losses when gradient noise at the optimum is small or zero.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate trajectories for planning, but their non-sequential structure makes long-horizon reasoning at inference time difficult. Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion addresses this by combining trajectory diffusion with tree search. This paper identifies two major computational costs in that combination: sequential search operations and repeated denoising during simulated continuations, or rollouts.

Fast-MCTD tackles both costs. Its parallel component delays tree updates so multiple rollouts can proceed together, while redundancy-aware selection helps manage overlapping search work. Its sparse component coarsens trajectories to shorten rollouts. Together, these changes reduce the overhead of searching and generating candidate plans while retaining the underlying combination of diffusion and tree-based reasoning.

Experiments report speedups of up to 100 times over standard MCTD, with planning performance maintained or improved. On some tasks, Fast-MCTD even runs faster at inference than Diffuser, a method without search that produces weaker solutions in those comparisons. The results show that restructuring search and trajectory resolution can make this form of inference-time planning substantially more practical.
neurips-2025-fast-monte-carlo-tree-diffu.tldr: Fast-MCTD combines parallel search and coarser trajectories for up to 100× faster planning while maintaining or improving reported performance.

paragraphs: Joint image alignment places a collection of images into a shared coordinate system so corresponding semantic features occupy matching locations. Existing approaches can require lengthy training, large models, and extensive parameter tuning. FastJAM addresses these costs by organizing image correspondences into a graph and using that graph to predict the transformations needed for alignment.

The pipeline starts with pairwise matches from an existing image matcher. Rapid nonparametric clustering helps build a graph containing keypoint relationships within and across images. A graph neural network passes and combines correspondence information, then pools it at the image level to predict each image’s homography parameters. These parameters specify the transformations used to align the collection.

FastJAM also uses an inverse-compositional loss that removes the need for a regularization term on predicted transformations, along with the tuning associated with that term. Across several benchmarks, the authors report better alignment quality than modern comparison methods and computation reduced from minutes or hours to seconds. The results support a graph-based route to faster joint alignment.
neurips-2025-fastjam-a-fast-joint-alignm.tldr: FastJAM uses a graph of image correspondences to improve joint alignment quality while reducing reported computation to seconds.

paragraphs: Federated learning can combine knowledge from clients while keeping their private data local. When clients use different model architectures, however, their knowledge is represented differently. The authors argue that distilling only output predictions does not adequately compensate for the resulting knowledge bias, and that combining heterogeneous federated learning with conventional ensemble distillation can make training unstable.

FedFD transfers internal feature information through a feature-based ensemble distillation procedure. The server’s global model maintains a separate projection layer for each client architecture, allowing features from different kinds of models to be aligned. Orthogonal reparameterization of these projections is used to mitigate architecture-related knowledge bias and improve how much useful information is distilled.

The central idea is to make heterogeneous internal representations compatible before using them to teach the global model. Extensive experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art comparison methods. These findings support the proposed aligned feature-distillation approach in the evaluated settings, while the architecture-specific projection layers explain how the method accommodates differences among client models.
neurips-2025-feature-distillation-is-the.tldr: FedFD aligns client features through orthogonal projections to improve knowledge distillation across heterogeneous federated models.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a fluid flow from a small number of sensors requires both a good prediction model and informative sensor locations. Practical deployment limits make this difficult. The paper studies reconstruction under realistic conditions, motivated by prior methods that often assume simplified domains, prescribed governing equations, idealized synthetic flows, or unrestricted sensor placement.

The reconstruction model is a directional transport-aware graph neural network. It explicitly represents flow direction and the movement of information, making these properties part of how measurements inform the reconstructed field. The authors also find that conventional placement strategies frequently select suboptimal sensor configurations, so improving the reconstruction network alone does not address the full problem.

To optimize placement, they introduce Two-Step Constrained PPO, a reinforcement-learning procedure that accounts for flow variability and the reconstruction model’s differing performance across sensor layouts. Experiments under realistic assumptions benchmark both components and report significant improvements over existing methods. The work treats sensing and reconstruction as connected choices: the usefulness of a sensor layout depends partly on the model interpreting its measurements.
neurips-2025-flow-field-reconstruction-w.tldr: A transport-aware graph network and constrained sensor-placement policy jointly improve flow reconstruction under realistic conditions.

paragraphs: Recovering missing values in a time series requires preserving the broader structure of the data as well as individual numbers. The authors observe that, when many values are missing, models trained with pointwise reconstruction losses can perform well during training yet produce poor imputations at inference. Their internal representation distributions also become distorted, suggesting that local numerical accuracy alone provides insufficient guidance.

Glocal-IB adds global guidance through a model-agnostic training framework based on the information bottleneck. Its Global Alignment loss comes from a tractable approximation to mutual information. The loss encourages representations of artificially masked inputs to align with representations of their originally observed counterparts, helping retain structure despite the missing information.

This objective is intended to preserve both local details and global organization while suppressing noise introduced by missing values. Experiments on nine datasets report consistently improved imputation performance and better-aligned latent representations. The findings support training objectives that explicitly stabilize representations under missingness, particularly when the amount of missing data makes pointwise reconstruction vulnerable to overfitting.
neurips-2025-glocal-information-bottlene.tldr: Glocal-IB improves time-series imputation by aligning masked-input representations with observed counterparts while preserving local details.

paragraphs: Gradient descent is often analyzed with small steps that reduce the objective at every update. This paper examines a setting where allowing temporary increases can accelerate convergence: logistic regression with L2 regularization and linearly separable data. The method remains ordinary gradient descent with a constant step size; the change is to use a sufficiently large step.

For this setting, the authors improve the iteration dependence from approximately the condition number to its square root, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The larger steps produce a nonmonotonic objective trajectory, so steady improvement at each update is not required for the faster overall rate. They also extend the acceleration result to population-risk minimization for separable distributions, improving the best-known upper bounds for reaching a near-optimum.

The paper further characterizes the largest step size permitting local convergence. In special scenarios, this threshold also determines global convergence. These results extend earlier large-step analysis from convex problems whose minimizers lie at infinity to strongly convex problems with finite minimizers, clarifying where this acceleration can occur.
neurips-2025-large-stepsizes-accelerate-.tldr: For L2-regularized logistic regression on separable data, large constant steps accelerate gradient descent despite nonmonotonic objective values.

paragraphs: Vision-language models need to reason about images while producing text efficiently and following output constraints. LaViDa explores discrete diffusion as a basis for these models. Diffusion supports parallel decoding and can use context on both sides of missing text, offering mechanisms for faster generation and controlled text completion.

The authors attach a vision encoder to diffusion language models and jointly fine-tune the components for multimodal instruction following. They introduce complementary masking to support training, a prefix key-value cache to improve inference efficiency, and timestep shifting to improve sampling quality. These techniques address the practical challenge of turning a diffusion language model into a capable multimodal system.

Experiments report competitive or superior results relative to autoregressive vision-language models on benchmarks including MMMU. On COCO captioning, LaViDa improves over Open-LLaVa-Next-8B by 4.1 CIDEr with a 1.92× speedup. It also reports a 59% improvement on Constrained Poem Completion. The findings support diffusion as a practical alternative with adjustable speed-quality tradeoffs and useful bidirectional generation capabilities.
neurips-2025-lavida-a-large-diffusion-la.tldr: LaViDa combines diffusion language models with vision encoding to deliver competitive multimodal performance and flexible, controllable generation.

paragraphs: An embodied agent benefits from predicting how its actions will change what it observes. Video-based world models can support this prediction, but models without memory of content outside the current view can produce inconsistent long-horizon simulations. That is particularly problematic in partially observed environments, where much of the scene is temporarily invisible.

This paper introduces a world model with an explicit, persistent 3D memory. A video diffusion model generates future observations containing both color and depth. The generated content is then aggregated into a 3D map, and the map conditions subsequent video generation. Previously generated spatial content therefore remains available even when it is absent from the agent’s current images.

The authors show that this feedback between video generation and spatial memory enables more consistent long-horizon simulation of seen and unseen parts of the environment. They also demonstrate the model in downstream planning and policy-learning applications. The contribution ties continuity in generated observations to a maintained spatial representation, giving simulated future actions a more persistent world in which to unfold.
neurips-2025-learning-3d-persistent-embo.tldr: A persistent 3D map gives a video world model spatial memory, improving long-horizon simulation and supporting planning and policy learning.

paragraphs: Claims that language models surpass elite competitive programmers depend on what problems are tested and how success is interpreted. LiveCodeBench Pro revisits those claims using problems from Codeforces, ICPC, and IOI. The benchmark is continuously updated to reduce the likelihood that evaluation problems have already appeared in model training data.

Olympiad medalists label every problem by algorithmic category and examine failed model submissions line by line. This combines outcome measurement with expert analysis of how solutions break down. Without external tools, the best evaluated model achieves 53% first-attempt success on medium-difficulty problems and 0% on hard problems, areas where expert humans remain strong.

The analysis finds that models handle implementation-heavy tasks more successfully than nuanced algorithmic reasoning and complex case analysis. Failed solutions can include confidently incorrect explanations. The authors interpret high performance as appearing largely driven by implementation precision and tool assistance. Their benchmark exposes a remaining gap to human grandmasters while providing more specific diagnostic information than a single aggregate programming score.
neurips-2025-livecodebench-pro-how-do-ol.tldr: Expert analysis in LiveCodeBench Pro reveals substantial remaining gaps in LLM algorithmic reasoning, especially on hard problems without tools.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning of large language models becomes difficult when participating clients have different computing capacities. The computational burden can leave slower clients lagging behind and reduce overall training efficiency. Layer-wise Efficient Federated Fine-tuning, or LEFF, addresses this by choosing which model layers each client updates according to the resources it can provide.

The method combines resource-aware layer selection with importance-driven layer sampling. Capacity-based selection reduces work assigned to constrained clients, helping mitigate the straggler effect. Importance-based sampling prioritizes layers with greater influence on model performance. Together, these mechanisms connect the allocation of client computation to both hardware capability and the expected usefulness of updating particular parts of the model.

The theoretical analysis establishes an O(1/√T) convergence rate. Experiments across diverse datasets report better computational efficiency and model performance than existing federated fine-tuning methods, particularly when client capabilities vary. The findings support selective layer updating as a way to make distributed adaptation more efficient while preserving the performance goals of fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-llm-at-network-edge-a-layer.tldr: LEFF adapts layer updates to client capacity and layer importance, improving reported federated fine-tuning efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: Generating several people in one image requires coordinating their identities, number, and actions. MultiHuman-Testbench provides a dedicated evaluation setting for this combination. It contains 1,800 samples with prompts spanning simple to complex human actions, paired with 5,550 unique face images sampled uniformly to support diversity across age, ethnic background, and gender.

The benchmark also supplies human-selected pose-conditioning images that match the prompts. Its evaluation suite separately measures face count, identity similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection. These dimensions make it possible to assess whether a generator satisfies different parts of a multi-person request, rather than treating an image’s overall plausibility as sufficient evidence of success.

The authors evaluate zero-shot and training-based methods, including approaches with and without regional priors. They also introduce image and region isolation techniques using human segmentation and Hungarian matching, reporting significant gains in identity similarity. The benchmark and accompanying methods provide a standardized way to investigate where multi-human generation succeeds and where preserving individual identities remains difficult.
neurips-2025-multihuman-testbench-benchm.tldr: MultiHuman-Testbench evaluates identity, count, prompts, and actions in multi-person image generation and introduces techniques that improve identity similarity.

paragraphs: Chemical-process monitoring depends on recognizing unusual behavior in sensor measurements over time. Developing detection methods is difficult because industrial data are usually proprietary, while simulated processes do not generally provide an adequate substitute. NoBOOM addresses this data-access problem with a collection of real chemical-process datasets for time-series anomaly detection.

The collection includes labeled measurements from an operating process at BASF and data from several laboratory-scale and pilot-scale plants. For the smaller plants, the authors provide detailed information about equipment configuration, process operation, and anomaly events. This context supports more differentiated analysis of detection methods by connecting sensor patterns to the processes and events that produced them.

Some details of the industrial process cannot be shared, a stated constraint on that part of the collection. The authors also examine common benchmark problems, including whether detection tasks are trivial or biased, to demonstrate the data’s complexity. The contribution supplies real-process evidence and contextual documentation for studying anomaly detection in a domain where representative public data are difficult to obtain.
neurips-2025-noboom-chemical-process-dat.tldr: NoBOOM supplies labeled real chemical-process data and process context for evaluating industrial anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification seeks the option with the highest expected reward while controlling the probability of a wrong answer. This paper studies binary, Bernoulli rewards under global differential privacy. Privacy changes how much evidence can safely be extracted from observations, creating a gap between known sample requirements and the guarantees achieved by existing algorithms.

The authors tighten the lower bound using an information quantity that balances Kullback–Leibler divergence against total variation distance scaled by the privacy budget. They use the corresponding transportation costs to design both a stopping rule and a Top Two sampling rule. Private mean estimates are computed with arm-dependent geometric batching, supported by new concentration results for Laplace noise and its combination with Bernoulli observations.

For every privacy budget, the algorithm’s asymptotic expected sample complexity matches the new lower bound within a multiplicative constant smaller than eight. Reported comparisons also favor it over existing algorithms meeting the same correctness and global-privacy requirements. The work substantially narrows the theoretical efficiency gap without claiming an exact match to the lower bound.
neurips-2025-optimal-best-arm-identifica.tldr: A new private best-arm algorithm matches a tighter sample-complexity lower bound asymptotically within a factor smaller than eight.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience from earlier tasks to make learning on new tasks faster. This paper investigates that idea for linear bandits, where a learner must make choices while learning about rewards from feedback. The central question is how a representation learned across related tasks can reduce the information needed to handle additional tasks.

The analysis considers T linear bandit tasks with d-dimensional inputs that share a common low-dimensional linear representation. Under this shared-structure assumption, the authors provide algorithms for two connected stages: learning useful common features from multiple tasks and transferring those features to previously unseen tasks. The representation provides a common basis for carrying knowledge between the two stages.

The paper establishes that its algorithms are provably fast and sample-efficient, then examines the theoretical results through numerical experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets against benchmark algorithms. Its contribution is a principled treatment of both acquiring and reusing shared bandit features. The efficiency results are grounded in the assumption that related tasks share a low-dimensional linear structure.
neurips-2025-provably-efficient-multi-ta.tldr: The paper gives provably efficient algorithms for learning shared low-dimensional bandit features and transferring them to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Reward alignment at inference time steers a generative model toward outputs that satisfy a desired objective. Sequential Monte Carlo methods do this by managing a collection of candidate samples, or particles, throughout denoising. This paper focuses on their starting points: a standard Gaussian initialization may poorly cover regions relevant to the reward, reducing sampling efficiency.

Ψ-Sampler initializes particles from a reward-aware posterior instead. To make this sampling practical in high-dimensional latent spaces, it incorporates preconditioned Crank–Nicolson Langevin sampling. This algorithm combines proposals designed to remain robust with dimension and dynamics informed by gradients. The resulting initialization brings reward information into the process before the subsequent SMC denoising stages.

The authors demonstrate that reward-aware initialization significantly improves alignment and report consistent gains across layout-to-image generation, generation with requested quantities, and aesthetic-preference generation. The contribution identifies initial particle selection as an important part of inference-time steering. Its experiments support using a more informative starting distribution to improve how effectively later sampling work pursues the reward.
neurips-2025-psi-sampler-initial-particl.tldr: Ψ-Sampler improves inference-time reward alignment by initializing SMC particles from a reward-aware posterior using pCNL sampling.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution with several separated modes can be difficult for methods that make local moves. Simulated tempering is a strategy for addressing this problem. This paper develops theory for simulated tempering paired with an arbitrary local Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler, focusing on target distributions formed as mixtures.

The main result is a decomposition theorem that lower-bounds the algorithm’s restricted spectral gap, a quantity used to analyze sampling convergence. Working with this restricted quantity broadens the analysis to situations where the usual spectral gap is difficult to bound or becomes degenerate. The theorem therefore provides an alternative route to convergence guarantees in mixture-sampling problems.

The authors apply the result to simulated tempering with random-walk Metropolis–Hastings for Gaussian mixtures. Their complexity bound grows polynomially with separation between modes and logarithmically with inverse target accuracy measured in total variation distance. It grows exponentially with dimension, an explicit qualification of the guarantee. The result clarifies how separation, accuracy, and dimensionality enter this particular sampling analysis.
neurips-2025-restricted-spectral-gap-dec.tldr: A restricted-spectral-gap theorem expands simulated-tempering analysis, yielding Gaussian-mixture bounds with exponential dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Commuting origin-destination flows describe daily movement between areas, but collecting them through travel surveys is costly and raises privacy concerns. This paper investigates publicly available satellite imagery as a source of information for generating these flows. The authors report that its urban semantic signals provide over 98% of the expressiveness of traditional, harder-to-collect multisource urban data.

GlODGen first uses vision-language geographic foundation models to extract mobility-related urban features from satellite images. It combines those features with population data to represent individual regions. A graph diffusion model then generates flows between regions. This pipeline connects visible urban structure and population information to the relationships needed to model commuting.

Experiments cover six representative cities across four continents and report strong generalization across varied urban environments, with generated flows highly consistent with observed mobility data. The released automated tool integrates data acquisition, curation, feature extraction, and flow generation. The stated ambition is worldwide applicability; the empirical evidence comes from the cities and continents evaluated.
neurips-2025-satellites-reveal-mobility-.tldr: GlODGen combines satellite-derived urban features, population data, and graph diffusion to generate commuting flows across diverse cities.

paragraphs: An object detector trained on one source domain may struggle when the visual environment changes. The authors attribute part of this problem to spurious correlations: a model can rely heavily on simple cues such as color while underusing more stable features such as object contours. Data augmentation alone may leave these dependencies unresolved when domain knowledge is limited.

Cauvis addresses the problem with causal visual prompts. A cross-attention module integrates visual prompts to reduce bias from spurious features. A dual-branch adapter then separates causal and spurious features while using high-frequency feature extraction for domain adaptation. These components address both limited domain coverage and the mixing of useful and misleading information within the prompts.

On single-source domain-generalized object detection datasets, Cauvis reports state-of-the-art results with gains of 15.9–31.4% over existing domain-generalization methods. It also shows robustness advantages in environments with complex interference. The findings support feature-focused prompt adaptation as a way to improve transfer from a single training domain to unseen target domains.
neurips-2025-towards-single-source-domai.tldr: Cauvis combines visual prompts and feature disentanglement to improve object detection in unseen domains after single-domain training.

paragraphs: A language model can solve a problem successfully without necessarily helping a person understand how to solve it. This paper treats the transfer of knowledge from an AI collaborator to a human as a capability requiring its own evaluation. It introduces a conceptual framework and a user study involving 118 participants to measure that capability.

The study separates collaboration from implementation. Participants first discuss problem-solving strategies with a language model, then implement solutions independently. This two-phase setup is designed to isolate how the model’s reasoning influences human understanding, using the person’s subsequent independent work as evidence of what the interaction enabled them to learn.

Model benchmark performance correlates with collaborative outcomes, but the relationship is inconsistent and includes substantial outliers. The authors interpret this as evidence that knowledge transfer needs dedicated optimization. Their analysis also identifies behavioral and strategic factors mediating successful transfer. By releasing the study’s code, data, and evaluation framework, they provide a basis for assessing how well models communicate usable reasoning to human collaborators.
neurips-2025-when-models-know-more-than-.tldr: A 118-person study shows that model benchmark strength inconsistently predicts how effectively humans learn from collaborating with it.
